implementation_notes: Schema-first and type-inferring: declare the request shape once with z.object, call safeParse, and the discriminated union forces the caller to handle the failure branch, where error.issues lists every problem with a typed path - parse() throws and is the fail-fast form. Choose it when the schema should also produce the static types; the decorator variant fits when the checks belong on the DTO class itself.
pitfalls: Modelling the boundary with parse() and catching ZodError defeats the discriminated union and reintroduces fail-fast.
error.issues is ZodIssue[]; mapping it into the API's error contract must preserve issue.path as an array rather than a joined string.
An inline schema rebuilt per call recompiles on every request and loses the single source of truth - hoist it to module scope.

variants.name: class-validator decorators
variants.implementation_notes: The decorator style keeps the constraints next to the fields: annotate the DTO class, then validate(instance) resolves to an array of ValidationError objects (each with property, constraints and optional nested children), so an empty array means valid and every failed property is present; NestJS's ValidationPipe builds its 400 responses from exactly this array, with stopAtFirstError defaulting to false. Choose it when the DTO class is the contract and DI-based custom validators are wanted.
pitfalls: Decorators only run when the class is instantiated - pass plainToInstance or new, not the raw JSON object.
ValidationError.children nests the errors of nested objects; ignoring it drops the failures of array items and sub-objects.
Without whitelist/forbidNonWhitelisted in NestJS's pipe, unknown properties pass through unvalidated - the DTO only checks what it declares.
